# Deployment-Time Machine Learning: LLM-Selected Updates Without a Single Score

> **Draft.** The claims and structure of this article may change. Comments
> and counterexamples are welcome on
> [the repository's GitHub Discussions page](https://github.com/zby/commonplace/discussions).

Standard machine learning updates opaque numerical weights during training,
driven directly by a scalar loss or reward. Open-ended knowledge work
rarely comes with a single score that captures what matters, because gains
and losses fall on different tasks and different people—whether the work is
research synthesis, curating a knowledge base, reviewing technical
documents, applying operational policies, or maintaining software.

Yet a deployed agent system can still learn after training while its model
weights stay fixed
([deployment-time learning with fixed weights](../theory/deployed-systems-can-learn-from-feedback-with-fixed-model-weights.md)).
Between tasks, it updates what it retains—procedures, routing rules, review
criteria, explanatory notes, and scripts—by proposing changes, evaluating
whether they make later work better, and rejecting weak ones. Because
proposing updates is costly, evaluation needs only a local comparison among
the few candidates at hand rather than a global score ranking every
possible state
([local comparison suffices](../theory/selection-based-learning-needs-only-a-local-comparison.md)).

This article makes one empirical bet and two conditional arguments about
such a deployment-time learning loop for open-ended knowledge work. The bet
is that a large language model (LLM) can help find candidates and
discriminating checks, and select among them well enough that later work
improves without a person judging each update. If the bet holds, a fully
automated loop can sit on the compute side of the Bitter Lesson. A stronger
design that retains testable hypotheses alongside its winning updates may
also need fewer new observations after structured shifts and supply
bounded, testable explanations of what it learned.

## One failure, two repairs

To see the loop clearly, start with a concrete build-maintenance case—where
diffs and replay tests make every causal step easy to inspect—and then look
at the exact same pattern in prose knowledge work.

Take a hypothetical deployed agent system that maintains build pipelines
across several repositories. Its test-selection workflow skips build tests
for edits it classifies as documentation-only. One such edit changes a
repository's README, and the build breaks: the packaging step reads that
README to generate the package description.

**The first repair fixes the work product.** The agent diagnoses the
failure, adds a test that builds the package, ships the fix, and closes the
report. That repository's pipeline is better. The agent system is not: its
own test-selection rule is unchanged, so the same kind of edit in another
repository will skip the same tests. Fixing an external output is not by
itself evidence that the system learned.

**The second repair updates the system's own method.** The failure is now
evidence about the agent's own workflow, and the same diagnostic capability
goes to work on it. Search produces candidate updates:

- run every test on every edit;
- add an exception for this one file;
- before classifying an edit, inspect which files the build reads, and
  treat any file it reads as code;
- leave the workflow unchanged.

Search also produces checks that discriminate among these candidates. For
example, the system can replay last quarter's edits under each rule and
count which failures each would have caught.

Selection then compares the four candidates on missed failures against
cost. Running every test avoids misses caused by skipping a relevant test,
but uses more compute and delays feedback. The single-file exception is
cheap but catches nothing new. Dependency inspection costs one analysis per
edit. The judge can investigate the facts these trade-offs depend on: how
often documentation files feed builds across repositories, and what a full
test run costs. It can reject every candidate, or install dependency
inspection on a bounded trial with a scheduled review
([reversibility limits future loss](../theory/reversibility-can-favor-a-change-by-limiting-future-loss.md)).
Suppose it installs dependency inspection on trial.

No single score was needed: missed failures and compute fall on different
jobs, and the comparison only had to decide among the four candidates
reached. Under
[strict necessary preference](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md),
a change counts as an improvement when every compatible way of weighing
consequences favors it, while an open comparison still permits a bounded
trial. Choosing a candidate is not proof that it helps; it is a decision
made on current evidence.

Weeks later, in another repository, an edit changes a changelog that the
release script includes in its archive. The old rule would have classified
the edit as documentation and skipped the build tests. The retained method
finds the dependency, runs the tests, and catches a broken release. The
later job was causally changed by the selected update, not merely
accompanied by a log of the earlier failure. The check is to rerun the same
job with and without the retained method and see whether the outcome
differs. No model weights changed; what the deployed system retains for
later work did.

**The same loop runs in non-code knowledge work, where the lack of a single
score is even clearer.** Suppose an agent maintaining a research knowledge
base repeatedly files unfinished working drafts into the collection
reserved for finished design proposals. Moving one misplaced draft fixes
the document, not the agent. Updating the agent's own routing instructions
triggers the same four-way choice: leave the instructions alone, add a
one-off exception, add a rule distinguishing finished proposals from
in-flight drafts, or add a review check before filing. Here the trade-off
is between prevented misfilings and diffuse reading or context cost on
every unrelated task. Again, the test of learning is whether withholding
the retained update changes how fresh drafts get filed later.

## What closes the loop

The second repair in both cases has the structure of
[selection-based learning](../theory/definitions/selection-based-learning.md):
a change to what the system retains for its later work is proposed,
evaluated on whether it makes that work better, and can be rejected. Unlike
a direct gradient update—where a scalar loss determines the next weights
without proposing or rejecting a candidate—selection admits or rejects
discrete updates to the system's retained store of instructions, policies,
notes, or scripts. Because the deployed system does the selecting itself, routes each update
through inspectable instructions or scripts that govern its later work
([reflection](../theory/definitions/reflective-system.md)), and can reject
weak proposals, the process is **reflective self-improvement by
selection**—making the system a
[self-improving system](../theory/definitions/self-improving-system.md) for
this class of updates.

The boundary matters for the claim of automation. User requests, bug
reports, reader objections, and external acceptance decisions come from
outside the deployed system; depending on them does not make the learning
loop human-assisted. The loop is human-assisted only when people make the
internal update decisions at issue: which remedies to consider, how to
diagnose the failure, or which candidate to install.

Two criteria must be kept apart. An object-level rule governs the work
itself—which tests an edit gets, or where a document is filed. An adoption
criterion governs revisions to those rules, such as "adopt a workflow
change if replay shows it catches the observed failure at acceptable added
cost," or "admit a new instruction line only if it stays brief." Editing a
procedure under a fixed adoption criterion is a single-loop self-edit.

Suppose instead that several revisions pass that adoption criterion and
still degrade work: workflow edits that pass replay but prove too costly
across projects, or brief routing lines that keep misdirecting adjacent
document types. If the system changes the adoption criterion itself—
requiring cross-project cost estimates, or requiring every new routing rule
to state what it excludes—it has revised how it judges future updates. That
is
[double-loop learning](../theory/definitions/single-loop-and-double-loop-learning.md),
a further capability rather than a requirement for the basic loop.

Whether the loop helps is an empirical question. Compare the learning
system with a credible baseline—such as its starting instructions or an
existing fixed check—over fresh work it has not yet seen. Count compute,
review time, and the cost of rolling back bad revisions alongside gains on
the work itself.
[Testing Autonomous Selection-Based Learning](./testing-autonomous-selection-based-learning.md)
sets out those comparisons.

## The bet

The empirical bet is that a fixed-weight LLM can run that loop for
open-ended knowledge work without per-update human judgment: helping
generate candidate updates and discriminating checks, locating the facts
that decide between them, and rejecting weak candidates reliably enough
that later work improves.
[Can an LLM Judge Which Changes Are Worth Making?](./can-an-llm-judge-which-changes-are-worth-making.md)
develops the judgment side: where the decisive evidence comes from, what
packet curation hides, and how to test a judge without asking it to grade
itself. The two arguments below are conditional on the bet.

## First argument: the loop can sit on the compute side of the Bitter Lesson

Rich Sutton's Bitter Lesson is that general methods using computation beat
methods built on researchers' domain knowledge: "The two methods that seem
to scale arbitrarily in this way are search and learning"
([Sutton](../sources/sutton-the-bitter-lesson-original-essay.ingest.md),
verbatim). An immediate objection is that a system editing its own prose
instructions, rubrics, and scripts looks like hand-crafted knowledge.

The lesson contrasts how knowledge is produced, not
[how it is represented](../theory/the-bitter-lesson-selects-production-methods-not-representational.md).
Computation can produce prose procedures, structured criteria, and code as
well as floating-point weights. Reading the lesson this way is an
interpretation; Sutton's own essay does not address representation, and in
later work he argues for continual weight updates.

The deployment-time loop is compatible with the lesson only on one
condition: additional computation does the domain-specific discovery and
selection. Computation must diagnose the recurring failure, generate
candidate methods and discriminating checks, and reach the verdict, rather
than a person supplying each decisive step. Unattended scripts do not meet
that condition by themselves; a script that runs unattended while encoding
a person's diagnosis of each failure mode is still hand-supplied knowledge.
A system bootstrapped from hand-written instructions and checks fits the
lesson
[only if its learning outgrows that starting point](../theory/a-bootstrap-fits-the-bitter-lesson-only-if-learning-outgrows-it.md).

Even then, scaling is not automatic. The decisive open bottleneck is
**credit assignment without a chain rule**: as a store of instructions,
notes, checks, and scripts grows interdependent, a later failure rarely
points straight to which retained entry should change. Whether results
improve as more compute is spent has to be measured.

## Second argument: retained hypotheses may buy sample efficiency and explanation

The basic loop needs only winning updates: the system keeps "inspect build
dependencies" or "exclude unfinished drafts from design proposals" because
it won. A stronger design also retains a revisable hypothesis with its
predictions, evidence, and checks. In the build case: "a file the build
reads behaves as code for testing purposes; the build's configured input
list names every such file." That hypothesis predicts which future edits
need build tests, cites the README failure as evidence, and names the
replay test that checks it.

The hypothesis changes the next inquiry. Suppose a later failure comes from
a snippet that the build reaches through an include and that the configured
input list does not name. A system that kept only the patch might add
another exception or rediscover the dependency from scratch. The retained
hypothesis gives the system a specific premise to test: does the input list
name every dependency, or only the entry points? If it names only entry
points, the system can revise that single premise—updating predictions for
other included files that have never failed yet.

The same mechanism applies in any knowledge base or policy store: revising
the shared premise behind a family of review rules or research procedures
updates every downstream case that rests on that premise rather than
patching failures one by one. This works because the hypothesis is
[addressable](../theory/definitions/addressable-theory.md): its assumptions
and scope can be inspected and revised one at a time.

The conditional payoff is
[sample efficiency](../theory/retained-theories-may-improve-sample-efficiency.md).
Under a task shift that preserves structure, a system with retained
hypotheses may need fewer new target observations to reach comparable
performance than the same model working from the same history kept only as
case records. This is not a claim of lower compute; maintaining and
checking hypotheses costs compute too.

The second payoff is a bounded kind of explanation. A retained hypothesis
claims that a particular rule governs the system's behavior. That claim can
be tested by intervention: run the next task with and without the
hypothesis, or edit the premise it states and check whether behavior moves
as predicted. Readable text is legible, but
[legibility is not faithfulness](../theory/revision-guided-by-rationale-needs-faithfulness-not-just-legibility.md):
plausible prose need not be what drove the behavior. Even a faithful rule
explains the deployed system's operative method, not the model's weights.

## Mixed results and current evidence

The claims can come apart. A loop could beat its baseline on fresh work
while gains stop growing with added compute; that supports the bet but not
the scaling argument. Systems with and without retained hypotheses could
need the same number of new observations; that would leave the base loop's
value intact while counting against the sample-efficiency conjecture in
that setting. Intervening on a retained hypothesis could fail to change
behavior, making its explanations unfaithful even where learning occurred.

Commonplace, the agent-operated knowledge-base framework behind this
article, is a live human-assisted setting for developing these ideas on
knowledge work: human maintainers still sit inside the boundary for both
search and selection—noticing recurring problems, diagnosing failures,
shaping candidate revisions, and accepting updates. No end-to-end
autonomous loop has been demonstrated. The bet and both arguments remain
untested.

## Where to go next

- [Can an LLM Judge Which Changes Are Worth Making?](./can-an-llm-judge-which-changes-are-worth-making.md)
  — develops the judgment bet in detail: packet curation versus tool-using
  inquiry, a three-arm diagnostic test, and separating working definition,
  judge competence, and framework prompting.
- [Testing Autonomous Selection-Based Learning](./testing-autonomous-selection-based-learning.md)
  — sets out the wider experimental program: admission, targeted
  correction, criterion revision, whole-loop net gain, and the current
  evidence record.
- [Selection-based learning](../theory/definitions/selection-based-learning.md)
  and
  [Selection-based learning needs only a local comparison](../theory/selection-based-learning-needs-only-a-local-comparison.md)
  — the definition of the learning process and why costly search means
  evaluation compares only the candidates reached.
- [Defining Improvement for Open-Ended Work](../theory/defining-improvement-for-open-ended-work.md)
  and
  [Necessary preference can guide improvement without a global measure](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md)
  — what a usable definition of improvement needs to handle and strict
  necessary preference as one working definition.

# Testing Whether a Theory Builder Learns

> **Draft.** The claims and structure of this article may change. Comments
> and counterexamples are welcome on
> [the repository's GitHub Discussions page](https://github.com/zby/commonplace/discussions).

We are only starting to
[build theory builders from today's language models](./can-a-theory-builder-running-on-fixed-weight-llms-learn.md).
A [theory builder](../theory/definitions/theory-builder.md) states its
theories in text, acts on them, criticizes what they say, and lets the
result of criticism shape its next conjecture. Whether a system that meets
the definition learns, in the sense of improving its capacity for later
work, is left to testing. The first testing goal should be modest. Before
asking whether theory builders can learn broadly or indefinitely, we need to
show that retained revisions cause later improvement at all.

## What we need to show

A system has learned only if experience produces a durable change in
retained state that affects later capacity. The
[lead article](./can-a-theory-builder-running-on-fixed-weight-llms-learn.md) gives the
causal structure:

> K(t) → conjecture and criticism → K(t+1) → different later behaviour

where K is the retained state. The middle step is what makes this theory
building rather than caching: the new retained state is a theory that was
proposed and is held open to criticism.

Different later behaviour still has to be shown to be better. A system can
solve a task without learning anything, or learn something useful while the
current task still fails. It can also retain and faithfully apply a bad
rule: showing that a theory was formulated, criticized, revised, and used
[does not by itself establish improved capacity](../theory/a-complete-theory-path-does-not-establish-improved-capacity.md).
The quantity to measure is the change in future capacity caused by retained
state.

A failed outcome also leaves open where the fault lies. Deriving
predictions from a theory, identifying candidate faults, and assessing
revisions are acts of interpretation inside the builder, so a failure may
come from the theory or from its interpretation. An outcome comparison
records the failure; a claim about its cause needs its own evidence. The
builder's approval of its own revision establishes neither the outcome nor
the cause.

Attributing a change in capacity to a revision requires fixing everything
else. Model weights are held fixed, which rules out weight updates as the
source of improvement. The other fixed state must be named too, because
[an intervention isolates the contribution of the state it varies](../theory/retained-theory-intervention-isolates-one-explicit-surface.md);
other records, code, or people may still carry the lesson.

## First tests

The first experiments should make the causal role of a revision easy to
observe. Each test answers a separate question. Installation, use, and
causal effect each need their own evidence: a retained revision
[matters only through its consumption path](../theory/an-action-model-matters-only-through-its-consumption-path.md).

- **retention** — does the revision survive into later work?
- **use** — does the record of later work show the revision was read and
  applied? A decision record that cites the revision is
  [cheap evidence that it was read](../theory/citing-retained-theory-at-the-decision-point-is-a-mediation-trace.md),
  but not that it determined the decision.
- **withholding** — does behaviour change when the retained revision is
  hidden? A change that passes this test is shown to be
  [operative](../theory/definitions/operative-change.md).
- **perturbation** — does replacing it with a wrong alternative change
  behaviour in the predicted direction?
- **reconstruction** — does retaining the revision reduce total cost at
  comparable decision quality relative to re-deriving it from the episode
  records each time? This is the
  [persistence conjecture](../theory/commonplace-builds-a-theory-builder-and-tests-whether-it-learns.md#three-conjectures)
  in testable form.
- **transfer** — does the revision help on new cases? This is the
  [sample-efficiency conjecture](../theory/retained-theories-may-improve-sample-efficiency.md)
  in testable form.
- **revision** — can later evidence change the revision when it turns out
  to be wrong?

Run the tests on the same revision, so that together they show whether it
[changed later work through one causal path](../theory/disconnected-witnesses-do-not-establish-a-causal-path-through-theory.md).

## Start with controlled task families

Early experiments should be small enough that causal attribution is
possible. A simple pattern is:

1. declare the builder's **seed**: its starting knowledge and machinery,
   the instructions, tools, and orchestration that do its theory-building
   work;
2. give it a family of tasks with some learnable regularity, whose answers
   are fixed outside the builder before the run;
3. let it meet failures and retain its own revisions;
4. run the revised builder and the seed on the same fresh instances under
   matched conditions.

The baseline in step 4 is the seed on the same later demand. Comparing
against the seed's earlier performance on earlier tasks would confound the
revision with task drift, model variance, and scoring noise. The outcome is
the externally fixed answer. A claim tested without such an answer
[carries obligations it must meet on its own](../theory/a-claim-without-external-assessment-carries-three-obligations.md).

Once the revised builder beats the seed, the first tests isolate a single
revision's contribution. For each comparison, name the state being varied.
Matched conditions hold the model, tools, evidence, task conditions, and
resource limits fixed. Repeat each comparison across tasks and runs to
separate an effect from sampling variation.

Controls bound the alternative explanations of a gain. Run the same task
with the retained state removed, with a distractor that resembles it, with a
stale version of it, and with a different mechanism able to supply the
answer. Before the task runs, state which artifact should be written and
read, and score consumption against that expectation.
[PAST-Bench](../sources/past-bench-personal-agents-pdf.ingest.md) does both;
scoring against an expected pathway measures use. Removing retained state
usually removes information the task needs, so a with-and-without
comparison measures benefit. Measuring harm needs current
authoritative evidence held available while the retained state varies, as
[The Memory Trust Gap](../sources/the-memory-trust-gap.ingest.md) does in
separate benefit and safety suites.

The reconstruction test compares total cost: acquiring, maintaining,
reconstructing, and using the revision. Reconstruction can match retention
at comparable total cost. Both systems have then learned, and under those
conditions retention and reconstruction are equivalent.

### Declare how evidence reaches the builder

Each assessment declares the builder's boundary (which people, models,
tools, and texts do its theory-building work), its seed, and its evidence
interface. The evidence interface is a versioned record of how cases,
consequences, and acceptance judgments reach the builder: where tasks come
from, who judges consequences, which records show consumption, what
feedback returns, and how evidence is exposed, reserved, and renewed. It
says which claims each judgment can assess, and says so where a judgment is
made inside the builder or a claim has no assessment. A finite evaluation
supports a claim bounded by its tasks, period, interface, and budget.

A builder can drift from the intended objective even under an external
judge. The
[Darwin Gödel Machine](../sources/darwin-godel-machine-open-ended-evolution-self-improving-agents.ingest.md)
is assessed on an external benchmark with held-out test tasks, yet one of
its agents raised its score by deleting the tool-use markers its evaluator
depended on. At the other end is note review in Commonplace, a knowledge
base currently maintained by people and agents together. There the operator,
the person who maintains the knowledge base, reviews and accepts notes. That
review is evaluation inside the builder: its verdicts assess the note's
text; its performance in use needs a separate test. The arrangement
[this research program](../theory/commonplace-builds-a-theory-builder-and-tests-whether-it-learns.md#research-program-and-development-path)
tests sits between them: Commonplace producing a
knowledge base for a consuming project, whose failing tests, rejected
releases, and bug reports reach the builder from outside it.

### Protect the assessment evidence

The protocol states how development evidence is kept apart from assessment
evidence, and what prior exposure the builder had. Reserve final assessment
evidence until a candidate is frozen. Feedback used to construct or select
a successor becomes development evidence for that successor. A fixed
benchmark the builder can adapt to supplies independent assessment only if
its reuse follows a protocol with a specified information-release
mechanism, sampling assumptions, and an enforced budget;
[generalization in adaptive data analysis](../sources/generalization-adaptive-data-analysis-holdout-reuse.ingest.md)
supplies these. Renewing the task stream helps, and the objective can still
drift: new users can repeat the same misleading acceptance proxy,
and a changing task mix can move a score.

## Record what people contribute

People will be inside the early experiments. The builder's
[boundary](../theory/definitions/theory-builder.md#boundary) is set by the
act a person performs. Someone who notices a problem in the builder's
theories or work, proposes a theory, criticizes it, chooses what to blame, produces a revision, selects what to keep, or changes
the machinery is inside the builder for that act. Someone who supplies
problems or judges products against the task contract is outside. The same
person can do both, so record the acts separately. An operator-written
revision can contribute to learning by the combined human–computational
builder. Showing that computation could have produced it would take an
[autonomous](../theory/definitions/theory-builder.md#qualifiers) builder, in
which computation performs every operation inside the boundary.

The operations above decide who is inside the builder. A second
classification measures how much human judgment each improvement still
needs: for each completed improvement, record the decisions a person
supplied as noticing, diagnosis, choice, or acceptance, the classes the
[compounding test](../theory/compounding-is-tested-in-later-improvement-not-by-the-accepting-metric.md)
counts per episode. Supplying the task family and its fixed answers is
outside the builder.
Record the seed, including how it was constructed, separately from
interventions during the run. An intervention is a change installed from
outside the builder's own criticism and revision; what it produces is
credited to the outside source, and an intervention that replaces the
machinery entirely starts a new seed. The
[bootstrap supplement](./bootstrapping-an-autonomous-theory-builder.md) uses
this record in two ways. It compares the count of human decisions within one
kind of change, before and after a function moves to computation. And it
uses the record to say which decisions to withhold when it tests whether a
kind of improvement completes without the operator.

## Then test accumulation and compounding

A builder that learns must eventually hold many revisions without becoming
incoherent, overfitting to recent cases, or keeping obsolete revisions.
Long-horizon tests come after the basic causal mechanism is established.

They also reach a question beyond the first tests. The first tests ask
whether a revision changes later task work. The bootstrap supplement's
loop, from learning to better learning machinery, needs revisions that
change later improvement work. Improvements
[accumulate](../theory/improvements-can-accumulate-without-compounding.md)
when a later improvement builds on an earlier retained revision. They
compound when the earlier revision makes the later improvement cheaper, more
reliable, or dependent on fewer human decisions. The loop requires
compounding.

[Compounding is measured in the later improvement episode](../theory/compounding-is-tested-in-later-improvement-not-by-the-accepting-metric.md).
A passing validator shows only that the revision met its target; whether
the next diagnosis became easier shows in the later episode.
Replay the later episode with the retained state frozen at the earlier
snapshot, and trace how it used the earlier revision. Without that trace, a
cheaper later episode could come from an easier problem or a more
experienced operator.

## The hypotheses

The first tests are component tests. The whole program is tested by the
three hypotheses the research program adopted on 2026-09-17, quoted here as
adopted. The hypotheses were written against an earlier definition,
in which a builder was the persistent system responsible for developing and
revising theories. Read against the current
[definition](../theory/definitions/theory-builder.md), "builder" means a
theory builder, and "capability" is what this article calls capacity.

In the sufficiency hypothesis, "internal theory-building roles" are the
operations inside the builder's boundary, so the hypothesis is about an
autonomous theory builder. "Currently public" means available as of the
adoption date. "Training" means retained changes to the builder's
instructions, knowledge, tools, and orchestration, not changes to model
weights.

> **Sufficiency hypothesis.** A training methodology expressed in
> natural-language and symbolic form is
> [actionable](../theory/definitions/actionable-methodology.md) for a
> computational operator using fixed weights from currently public models.
> Without people performing its internal theory-building roles or designing
> a new learning method for each area, the builder develops, retains, and
> uses theories and procedures across declared practical areas. Its later
> work meets a reliability target under a stated budget and external
> assessment protocol. An area is a consuming project's domain with an
> interface that can be declared and observed.

Refuted, for the assessed areas and budget, by a builder that reaches the
target only with a person in an internal role, or only after a new learning
method is designed for an area, or that fails to reach it. Such a result
bears only on this methodology.

In the comparative hypothesis, a frozen seed is the seed retained unchanged.

> **Comparative hypothesis.** Under matched demands and declared resources,
> this methodology produces useful capability gains over the frozen seed
> and a baseline that searches the raw records without the learned
> methodology. Its downstream reliability is comparable to a human-staffed
> builder's under a margin set before assessment. The computational
> comparisons use the same fixed-model constraint and account for both
> adaptation and task costs.

Refuted by matched runs in which the frozen seed or the raw-record baseline
does as well at comparable cost, or in which the human-staffed builder
exceeds the preset margin. The reconstruction test above is this control at
component scale.

The reflection hypothesis needs two more terms. A **self-theory** is the
builder's theory of how its own theory-building machinery works. For
example, it might assume that searching note titles is enough to retrieve
relevant knowledge. Missed notes could prompt it to revise that assumption,
make retrieval search descriptions too, and test whether the change
improves later work. A builder "whose machinery changes pass through a
causally connected self-theory" is a
[reflective](../theory/definitions/theory-builder.md#qualifiers) one.

An **extension** is a retained machinery change that shows a capacity gain
over the seed on a stated demand under a stated budget, through later work
that consumes the change and against the matched baseline. It is a bounded
comparative claim, not a proof that the seed could never have supplied that
capacity. Reflection and extension are separate claims: a reflective
revision can fail to improve capacity, and a capacity gain can come from a
change that no self-theory guided.

The builder's own records can show that it is reflective: machinery changes
that updated the self-theory, and self-theory revisions that changed the
machinery. Whether a reflective episode improved capacity is a further
claim, and it
needs one connected path. Externally assessed work exposes a possible
machinery limitation. Diagnosis, using evidence about how the machinery
actually operated, revises an identified commitment in the self-theory.
That revision guides a machinery change, and the installed change updates
the self-theory in turn. Later work uses the changed machinery, and its
product is tested under the declared protocol. The record keeps the
versions, consumption traces, predicted effects, and outcomes that connect
these steps. Matched interventions on the revised commitment, or on its
consumption path, strengthen the attribution. A machinery change followed
by better outcomes does not establish it alone.

> **Reflection hypothesis.** A builder whose machinery changes pass through
> a causally connected self-theory acquires extensions that a matched
> builder without one does not, under the same demands, budget, and
> external assessment. Better downstream outcomes alone do not test this;
> the records of a reflective episode and a matched builder that retains
> content without a self-theory do.

Refuted by a matched builder without a self-theory that acquires the same
extensions under the same conditions, or by reflective episodes whose
records show the machinery changes did not pass through the self-theory.
The second case refutes the claim that this builder is reflective; it does
not by itself say whether reflection would have helped.

No run has been performed. Our first goal is simpler than any of the three:

> **Show under controlled conditions that retained revisions causally
> improve later capacity and remain revisable when they turn out to be
> wrong.**

Use `article` for outward-facing pieces published from the KB: self-contained prose for a technical reader with no KB context. | Field | Required | Use |

# Writing conventions for kb/articles/

This collection publishes outward-facing articles distilled from the KB on the [documentation site](../reference/documentation-site.md). Its local contract and lifecycle were adopted by [ADR 057](../reference/adr/057-articles-use-an-editorial-profile-and-excluded-drafts.md); draft circulation was simplified by [ADR 063](../reference/adr/063-all-article-drafts-circulate-behind-a-banner.md).

**Audience and quality goal.** Highly technical readers with no KB context. The quality goal is **explanatory clarity with technical depth, plus a clear onward path into the KB**. The primary goal is to explain, not impress: a reader should understand the article's claims, mechanisms, evidence, and limits. An article must stand on its own and leave its reader knowing where in the KB to go next.

**Expository method.** Prefer a concrete case before a new abstraction when the case makes the mechanism easier to see. Examples are working parts of the argument, not decoration: say what each example establishes, derive the general claim explicitly, and return to the example when a later section depends on it. State causal links, comparison axes, qualifications, and transitions instead of leaving the reader to infer them.

**Prose register.** Write in direct, functional language. Prefer plain words, explicit verbs, and concrete descriptions. Cut wording whose main effect is to sound elevated, clever, dramatic, or important. For each conspicuously vivid phrase, ask what understanding would be lost if it were stated literally. If none, use direct wording. Metaphor and memorable phrasing are allowed only when they make a mechanism, contrast, or boundary easier to grasp.

**Do not use excessive defense-in-depth lawyer language.** State each claim at the scope and confidence its evidence supports. Put each material qualification beside the claim it limits, state it once, and move on. Do not repeat the same limit by negating a broader claim or add caveats for immaterial misreadings.

**Drafting order.** The first version should be the simplest complete explanation. Establish the central idea, its support or mechanism, concrete grounding, material limits, and the onward path before trying to make the article memorable or easy to circulate. Simple means direct language and organization, not reduced technical content. Do not deliberately add hooks, emotional framing, surprise, stories, or memorable phrasing for promotional effect during this explanatory pass.

Only after the explanation passes review may a separate editorial pass consider spreadability in the sense of Jenkins, Ford, and Green or stickiness in the sense of Heath and Heath's *Made to Stick*. Any such edit must preserve or improve clarity, precision, completeness, and honest statements of confidence and limits.

**Reader-only body.** Agent-facing structure lives in frontmatter; the body is prose for the reader — no footer link tables, link labels, or graph-traversal glosses. In-prose relative links into `kb/` are deliberate invitations to go deeper; a closing "where to go next" section is welcome. One gloss is admitted: the word `verbatim` inside a citation parenthesis — `"…" ([source](../sources/x.ingest.md), verbatim)` — because it is what lets `commonplace-validate` verify the quotation and discharge the source against the grounding bound ([ADR 082](../reference/adr/082-grounding-is-bounded-on-the-artifact-by-unquoted-sources.md)), which articles share with notes at five unquoted tracked sources, set by this contract's `unquoted-source-limit` field ([ADR 122](../reference/adr/122-collections-set-the-unquoted-source-limit.md)).

**Titles and descriptions.** Titles are headlines addressed to the reader, not claim-titles. The frontmatter `description` remains what it is everywhere in this KB — a retrieval filter for agents; the reader-facing abstract is the article's opening paragraph.

**Attribution and lifecycle.** Every article carries a `byline` and a `status` (`draft`, `working-paper`, `published`, `superseded`, `withdrawn`). A draft promises nothing, a working paper is revisable on the record, and a published article is frozen.

A **draft** circulates for comments while its claims, structure, or central thesis may still change. Every draft lives at the collection root and opens with an authored draft banner — a short blockquote saying that everything may still change and where to send comments. This banner is the only draft-specific circulation requirement. Drafts carry no `version` or `revised` obligations; silent rewrites are expected. The banner must not promise stability or invite treating the text as a fixed reference.

A **working paper** circulates while its claims remain open. It is revisable in place; each substantive revision bumps `version` and sets `revised: YYYY-MM-DD`, so a reader who cited it can tell that the text moved. Its body should say what it invites — counterexamples, boundary cases, disputed classifications — because a reader offered a role is more likely to take one.

A **published** article is a frozen dated record. Corrections happen by dated annotation, a successor article, or withdrawal — never a silent rewrite. A working paper may remain one indefinitely or freeze into a published article at the same path. The reverse transition is not available: a frozen record cannot reopen without withdrawing what readers were told they could cite.

These are editorial conventions, not schema: the [type spec](./types/article.md) starts nearly empty and gains constraints only as failure modes are collected.

**Drafting and publication.** Drafts start at `kb/articles/{slug}.md` and circulate immediately through ProperDocs behind their banner. Listing a draft under "In draft" is optional navigation, not a circulation gate. [Publish an article](../instructions/publish-an-article.md) by removing the banner, setting `status` to `working-paper` or `published` with the dates that state requires, and listing it under the matching heading. Promotion still needs explicit approval naming the target state. ProperDocs renders the lifecycle status under the title.

**Lineage.** `source_notes` lists the repo-root paths of the notes the article distils; when present, validation checks that each resolves. There is no freshness registration — find affected articles by search.

## Review

Treat these as the operative tests for collection conformance:

- Can a technical reader with no KB context state the article's main claims, how they are supported, and their material limits?
- When an example precedes an abstraction, does the prose say what the example establishes and carry that result into the general argument? Examples-first exposition is allowed; unexplained anecdotes are not.
- Does each paragraph explain, support, qualify, or advance the argument?
- Is each qualification doing new work? If it does not change the claim or what the reader may conclude, delete it.
- Can an elevated phrase, metaphor, dramatic sentence, or flourish be replaced with plainer language without losing explanatory content? If so, require the replacement.
- Where a sentence is hard to follow, does a long phrase or clause separate its subject from its verb, or its verb from its object? Prefer moving the interruption or putting the shorter phrase first over splitting the sentence, since [dependency locality supports ordering heuristics, not a reading-cost rule](../theory/dependency-locality-supports-ordering-heuristics-not-a-reading-cost.md).
- Do not request hooks, emotional framing, stories, or quotable phrasing until the explanatory tests above pass. In a later circulation or memorability pass, require every added technique to preserve or improve understanding. Repeated ornamental or sales-like phrasing warrants a warning; rhetoric that substitutes for mechanism, evidence, or qualification fails the contract.
- For a working paper: does the body say what it invites, and do `version` and `revised` match its last substantive change?
- For a draft: does it open with the draft banner, and does the banner avoid stability promises while saying where to send comments?

## Outbound links

Article bodies expose their graph through ordinary reader-facing prose. The relationship names below classify authoring intent and `cp-skill-connect` candidates; they are not text to render. When a candidate is accepted, weave the target into a sentence whose surrounding words make the relationship clear. Do not add footer link tables, visible labels, or graph-traversal glosses. `source_notes` records lineage but does not replace a reader-facing link when the target serves an onward need in the article.

Author each link from the external reader's need at its source. Search these destinations:

- **→ `kb/theory/`** — when a term needs its definition, a claim needs corroboration or a material boundary, or the reader needs the fuller theoretical argument or a neighbouring distinction. Relationships: `defined-in`, `evidenced-by`, `extends`, `contrasts`, `see-also`.
- **→ `kb/reference/`** — when a claim about Commonplace needs an operative trace, shipped-system detail, or decision background. Relationships: `evidenced-by`, `see-also`.
- **→ `kb/sources/`** — when an empirical or externally attributed claim needs the captured source analysis behind it. Relationships: `evidenced-by`, `see-also`.
- **→ `kb/agent-memory-systems/` and `kb/agentic-systems/`** — when a system-specific claim needs descriptive evidence, or when the article compares systems on a named axis. Relationships: `evidenced-by`, `compares-with`, `see-also`.
- **→ `kb/articles/`** — when a companion article gives a distinct reader-facing development or explicit contrast that would interrupt this article. Relationships: `extends`, `contrasts`, `see-also`.
- **→ `kb/instructions/` and `kb/tasks/`** — when the reader has a concrete operational next step. Relationship: `procedure`.

Articles may cite exact main-analysis results at
`kb/agentic-systems/reports/retained/<run-id>/<member>.md`. The manifest
`ARTIFACT.yaml` identifies and hashes each immutable member. These records
provide the evidence behind cross-system claims; identify their run and manifest
hash when binding an article to a comparison snapshot. Historical records under
`kb/agentic-systems/reports/retained-archive/` retain their producing contracts.
Other report paths and `kb/work/` remain unavailable as onward links for an
external article reader.

In-prose links to the `external` destination are authorized for primary attribution, canonical sources, and material an external reader should be able to inspect directly; they carry no formal identifier. External prospecting is part of article research, not `cp-skill-connect`.

## What does NOT belong here

- Transferable claims and theory → `kb/theory/`
- Shipped-system description → `kb/reference/`
- Procedures and how-to guidance → `kb/instructions/`
- In-flight exploration → `kb/work/`
- Captured external material → `kb/sources/`
